replies.author: @RenardGarland
replies.text: @silkeotd7194 While international border crossings like bridges generally involve shared operational responsibilities, the assertion that one country can never fully control or exercise ultimate authority over a cross-border bridge overlooks standard legal, financial, and infrastructural frameworks. From a sovereign and legal perspective, every country retains total, absolute sovereignty over the portion of any international structure that rests within its own territory; co-operation is a practical administrative choice rather than an absolute restriction on control. When one nation fully funds, owns, constructs, and manages the essential physical infrastructure—including tolling, maintenance, and access roads—it effectively holds operational dominance over the entire crossing, even if customs officers from the adjacent country handle entry on their side of the border. Regarding international agreements, foreign policy and border governance are inherently subject to changing domestic laws, national security priorities, and elected leadership, meaning that renegotiating or altering terms when a project directly impacts domestic commerce and border security is a standard feature of state sovereignty rather than simply a failure to honor commitments. Ultimately, while day-to-day traffic requires mutual co-operation, sovereign control over national land and the legal right to regulate foreign-funded infrastructure within a country's borders remain paramount.

comments.author: @jamesdjbrown
comments.text:
The "Canada got played" reading skips what Ottawa was actually facing. Under the oeginal 2012 agreement, Canada collects every toll until its 6.4 billion is repaid, then splits with Michigan. That deal is still in force. What Trump did in February was refuse the presidential permit, a signature the bridge cannot open without, and demand half ownership of a bridge the U.S. put no money into. Canada gave up none of the ownership and none of the toll-setting authority. What it agreed to was a payment from federal funds equal to half of net revenues, tolls minus operating costs, for fifteen years, into a U.S. development fund.

Is this the best deal? No. Measured against 2012 Canada gave up real money. 

But look at who was on the other side of the table. Trump's record on honouring agreements, including ones he signed himself, is what it is. CUSMA was his deal and he tore into it anyway. Holding out for the 2012 terms assumed a counterparty who would eventually respect a contract, and nothing in the past two years supports that assumption. The realistic choice was a smaller concession now with the bridge open, or an indefinite standoff with a closed bridge and a president who would simply raise the ask. Ottawa smartly took the smaller loss. 

And that is the larger point. A crossing Canada paid for entirely, on its own permit timeline, was still hostage to one man's signature. The Gordie Howe is one more piece of evidence that Canada's exposure to the United States is a structural problem, not only a Trump problem, and the only durable answer is to depend on it less. Diversifying trade, ports, and supply routes is slow and expensive. So was the bridge. Canada built it anyway.

But the alternative was a six billion dollar bridge sitting closed indefinitely while the Ambassador kept charging up to $27 an axle and the Moroun family kept the monopoly Canada spent a decade breaking. The Gordie Howe opened at $12 an axle and the traffic is already shifting. Fifteen years from now the payments end and Canada still owns half of the second-busiest commercial crossing on the continent, and helps reduce the costs to Canadians who rely on the bridge to earn thier livelyhood.
